clinicalPearls: A group of severe inherited retinal dystrophies presenting in infancy with profound visual impairment, usually autosomal recessive
Caused by variants in many genes, including RPE65, CEP290, GUCY2D, CRB1, and others, each with characteristic features
Infants show poor visual behaviour, roving nystagmus, sluggish pupillary responses, and the oculodigital sign (eye-poking/pressing)
The electroretinogram is severely reduced or non-recordable early, which is key to the diagnosis
Fundus may look near-normal in infancy, later developing pigmentary retinopathy, vessel attenuation, and disc pallor
RPE65-associated disease is treatable with an approved subretinal gene therapy, making genetic diagnosis clinically actionable
Certain genotypes have systemic associations (e.g. CEP290 with ciliopathy features), so systemic evaluation may be warranted
reference.pathophysiology: Leber congenital amaurosis encompasses genetically heterogeneous defects that disrupt photoreceptor development or function and the visual (retinoid) cycle. In RPE65-related disease, for example, the retinal pigment epithelium cannot regenerate the chromophore needed to restore light sensitivity to photoreceptors, so phototransduction fails and photoreceptors degenerate. Other causative genes impair photoreceptor ciliary transport, guanylate cyclase signalling, or outer-segment structure. The common consequence is early and severe loss of rod and cone function, reflected in a profoundly abnormal electroretinogram and progressive retinal degeneration.
additionalDifferentials: Joubert and Senior-Loken syndromes and other ciliopathies with retinal involvement
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing via retinal dystrophy gene panels
Optical coherence tomography to assess retinal layer and photoreceptor integrity
Detailed dilated fundus examination and retinal imaging
Systemic evaluation (including renal and neurological) where a ciliopathy is suspected
Assessment of vision and refraction, noting frequent high hyperopia
redFlags: Systemic features suggesting an associated ciliopathy (renal impairment, neurological or developmental signs)
Rapidly progressive visual loss or atypical course prompting reassessment
Failure to consider a treatable genotype (e.g. RPE65) that has an approved therapy
reference.prognosis: Vision is severely impaired from infancy and most genotypes are progressive, though some are relatively stable; the prognosis is being transformed for RPE65-related disease by gene therapy, and genotype-specific trials are altering outlook for other subtypes.
pitfalls: Attributing infantile nystagmus and poor vision to cortical visual impairment without electrophysiology
Failing to obtain genetic testing and missing a treatable RPE65 genotype
Overlooking systemic ciliopathy associations that require renal or neurological monitoring
Not correcting the frequently high hyperopic refractive error
management: Establish the molecular genetic diagnosis, since genotype determines treatment eligibility and prognosis and identifies treatable subtypes
Offer subretinal gene therapy with voretigene neparvovec for confirmed biallelic RPE65-associated disease
Optimise residual vision with refractive correction of the frequent high hyperopia and provision of low-vision aids
Provide early visual rehabilitation, educational support and mobility training for children with profound impairment
Screen for systemic renal and neurological involvement where a ciliopathy such as CEP290-related disease is suspected
Offer genetic counselling for this usually autosomal recessive condition, with testing of at-risk relatives
Refer to a specialist inherited retinal disease centre and consider enrolment in genotype-specific therapeutic trials
